claim: Neuropixels probes enable researchers to simultaneously record hundreds of neurons with remarkably high signal to noise.
source: The advent of high-yield electrophysiology using Neuropixels probes is now enabling researchers to simultaneously record hundreds of neurons with remarkably high signal to noise.
evidence: This is stated as an established capability of Neuropixels probes in the abstract, drawing on general knowledge about the technology.

claim: Neuropixels probes have not been well-suited to use in freely moving mice.
source: However, these probes have not been well-suited to use in freely moving mice.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the abstract, based on the authors' assessment of existing technology.

claim: The AMIE device allows Neuropixels probes to be customized for chronically implanted experiments in freely moving mice.
source: We designed and implemented a novel device that allows Neuropixels probes to be customized for chronically implanted experiments in freely moving mice.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental data and methods described throughout.

claim: The AMIE approach enables recording hundreds of neurons during ethological behavior across weeks of experiments.
source: We demonstrate the ease and utility of this approach in recording hundreds of neurons during an ethological behavior across weeks of experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: The AMIE approach enables researchers to explant and reuse Neuropixels probes.
source: Importantly, our approach enables researchers to explant and reuse these valuable probes, a transformative step which has not been established for recordings with any type of chronically-implanted probe.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Place and grid cell dynamics have been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: Electrophysiology in freely moving rodents has been used to observe place and grid cell dynamics (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cortical dynamics during attentional control have been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: Electrophysiology in freely moving rodents has been used to observe place and grid cell dynamics (Hafting et al., 2005; O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), cortical dynamics during attentional control (Bolkan et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The role of oscillations during fear learning has been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: the role of oscillations during fear learning (Stujenske et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Whisking behavior during exploration has been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: whisking behavior during exploration (Kerekes et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effect of environmental context on neural activity has been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: the effect of environmental context on neural activity (Whitlock et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The control of sensory selection in divided attention has been observed using electrophysiology in freely moving rodents.
source: the control of sensory selection in divided attention (Wimmer et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recording from unrestrained mice enables researchers to investigate behaviors that involve natural movements.
source: recording from unrestrained mice enables researchers to investigate behaviors that involve natural movements and offers ethologically valid insight into neural activity (Juavinett et al., 2018; Markowitz et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Electrophysiology in freely moving animals is commonly performed with static electrode arrays or microdrives.
source: Electrophysiology in freely moving animals is commonly performed with static electrode arrays or microdrives (Okun et al., 2016; Vandecasteele et al., 2012; Voigts et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Static electrode arrays and microdrives are not at pace with the spatiotemporal coverage of Neuropixels probes.
source: These techniques have contributed much to the field, but are not at pace with the spatiotemporal coverage of cutting edge recording techniques, such as Neuropixels probes (Jun et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited work on Neuropixels.

claim: The Neuropixels linear recording shank can record from 384 contacts across 3.84 mm.
source: The linear recording shank can record from 384 contacts across 3.84 mm (selectable from 960 available sites on a 10 mm length shank).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the Neuropixels probe, representing established knowledge.

claim: The mouse brain is at most 6 mm deep.
source: In the mouse brain, which is at most 6 mm deep, this span of contacts means researchers can simultaneously record from more than half of the depth of the brain.
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about mouse brain dimensions.

claim: Neuropixels probes can record from more than half of the depth of the mouse brain.
source: In the mouse brain, which is at most 6 mm deep, this span of contacts means researchers can simultaneously record from more than half of the depth of the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the probe specifications and brain dimensions.

claim: Neuropixels probes have low baseline noise levels (<6 µV RMS).
source: Further, Neuropixels probes have low baseline noise levels (<6 µV RMS), comparable to other silicon probes (Steinmetz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a technical specification supported by citation.

claim: Neuropixels probes have on-site amplification and digitization.
source: However, Neuropixels probes also have on-site amplification and digitization, thereby enabling simultaneous recording of hundreds of cells across brain regions in an unprecedented low-noise, high-throughput manner.
evidence: This is a technical feature of Neuropixels probes, representing established knowledge.

claim: Methods have been developed to automatically sort spikes from Neuropixels recordings.
source: Importantly, methods have also been developed to automatically sort spikes from these recordings, and even correct for probe drift (Jaeyoon et al., 2017; Pachitariu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neuropixels probes have proved invaluable for neuroscientists conducting acute experiments in mice.
source: Neuropixels probes have already proved invaluable for neuroscientists conducting acute experiments in mice, or chronic experiments in freely moving rats (Jaeyoon et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2018; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neuropixels probes have proved invaluable for chronic experiments in freely moving rats.
source: Neuropixels probes have already proved invaluable for neuroscientists conducting acute experiments in mice, or chronic experiments in freely moving rats (Jaeyoon et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2018; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is limited work with Neuropixels probes in unrestrained mice.
source: However, there is limited work with these probes in unrestrained mice (Evans et al., 2018), likely because of the difficulty designing small, lightweight recording devices.
evidence: This is an assessment of the literature with one citation and inference about the reason.

claim: There is plentiful interest in behaviors and computations that involve movements of the animal's head in space.
source: Still, there is plentiful interest in behaviors and computations that involve movements of the animal's head in space (Vélez-Fort et al., 2018), foraging (Lottem et al., 2018), pup retrieval (Marlin et al., 2015), or naturalistic fear responses (Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is not an established method to recover Neuropixels probes after experiments in freely moving rats.
source: Further, although these probes have been very successful in freely moving rats (Jaeyoon et al., 2017; Krupic et al., 2018), there is not an established method to recover them after the experiment.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on the literature.

claim: Neuropixels probes cost $1000 each.
source: Given the cost ($1000 each, https://www.neuropixels.org/) and limited availability of the probes, many researchers will only be able to use them if it is possible to recycle them after experiments.
evidence: This is factual information about the cost of the probes from the cited source.

claim: The ability to recover Neuropixels probes would enable researchers to repeat their experiments in different animals.
source: The ability to recover these probes would enable researchers to repeat their experiments in different animals, boost the statistical power of their experimental findings, and thus enhance reproducibility of experimental data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of probe recovery.

claim: The current design of the Neuropixels probe has several components that need to be securely mounted onto the small mouse skull.
source: First, the current design of the probe has several components that need to be securely mounted onto the small mouse skull.
evidence: This is an observation about the technical challenges of the probe design.

claim: The sensitive onboard electronics of Neuropixels probes need to be protected while the mouse is in its home cage.
source: Further, these sensitive onboard electronics need to be protected while the mouse is in its home cage.
evidence: This is a practical consideration for chronic implants.

claim: The shank of the Neuropixels probe must be secured to ensure consistent recordings across weeks of recording.
source: Most importantly, the shank of the probe must be secured to ensure consistent recordings across weeks of recording.
evidence: This is a technical requirement for chronic recordings.

claim: Previous work required permanently mounting the biosensor using adhesive, which made it nearly impossible to remove the probe afterwards.
source: In previous work, this required permanently mounting the biosensor using adhesive, which was effective but made it nearly impossible to remove the probe afterwards (Okun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The AMIE device weighs ~1.5 g (with cement: ~2.0 g).
source: The entire AMIE device weighs ~1.5 g (with cement:~2.0 g) and is assembled from three parts: the Neuropixels probe, the internal mount (IM), and external casing (EC) (Figure 1A,B; Video 1).
evidence: This is a measurement reported by the authors.

claim: The AMIE device is assembled from three parts: the Neuropixels probe, the internal mount (IM), and external casing (EC).
source: The entire AMIE device weighs ~1.5 g (with cement:~2.0 g) and is assembled from three parts: the Neuropixels probe, the internal mount (IM), and external casing (EC) (Figure 1A,B; Video 1).
evidence: This is a description of the device design shown in Figure 1.

claim: The internal mount attaches directly to the Neuropixels PCB board with adhesive.
source: The IM attaches directly to the Neuropixels PCB board with adhesive and is the core of the assembly (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the assembly method shown in Figure 1.

claim: The internal mount attaches to the external casing via a rail system.
source: The IM attaches to the EC via a rail system (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the device design shown in Figure 1.

claim: During the implantation procedure, all adhesive binding the assembly to the rodent's skull exclusively contacts the external casing.
source: During the implantation procedure, all adhesive binding the assembly to the rodent's skull exclusively contacts the EC, which acts as a protective shell (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a description of the implantation procedure shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Neuropixels probe has a ~3 cm long flex cable attached to a 1 g headstage.
source: One difficulty in adapting the current Neuropixels design for freely moving experiments in mice is the ~3 cm long flex cable attached to a 1 g headstage (see Jaeyoon et al., 2017) for details).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the Neuropixels probe supported by citation.

claim: In early testing, suspending the flex and headstage above the mouse's head caused the flex to twist quickly.
source: In early testing, we suspended the flex and headstage above the mouse's head during recording. However, we found that the flex very quickly twisted, potentially damaging it.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' preliminary experiments.

claim: The AMIE encasing has a space for the headstage to be semi-permanently affixed.
source: With these observations in mind, we designed the encasing with a space for the headstage to be semi-permanently affixed.
evidence: This is a description of the design solution.

claim: The probe flex wraps in an 'S' shape behind the implant.
source: The probe flex wraps in an 'S' shape behind the implant, and attaches to the bottom (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the design shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The surgery to implant the probe and encasing typically takes ~3 hr.
source: The surgery to implant the probe and encasing typically takes ~3 hr (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a reported duration from the authors' experience.

claim: A headbar can be implanted during surgery without interfering with the encasing.
source: During this surgery, a headbar can also be implanted, which does not interfere with the encasing.
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure.

claim: The external casing is the only part of the assembly that is attached to the skull.
source: The external casing is the only part of the assembly that is attached to the skull (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a description of the implantation method shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mice were mobile with the Neuropixels AMIE by approximately 48 hr post-surgery.
source: By approximately 48 hr post-surgery, mice were mobile with the Neuropixels AMIE (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Implanted mice were typically agile and active even while tethered.
source: Even while tethered, implanted mice were typically agile and active (Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments shown in Video 2.

claim: Considerable overlap was apparent in the distribution of behavioral metrics for implanted and naive mice.
source: For all three metrics, considerable overlap was apparent in the distribution of values for implanted and naive mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Implanted mice moved slightly less and were slightly slower than naive mice, but the differences failed to reach significance.
source: Although implanted mice moved slightly less and were slightly slower, the differences failed to reach significance for any metric.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: The mouse with the highest max acceleration was implanted.
source: In fact, the mouse with the highest max acceleration was implanted (Figure 3D, middle panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Overhead visual looming stimuli are known to elicit strong escape responses in mice.
source: To examine stimulus driven behavior, we measured responses to overhead visual looming stimuli (Figure 3E), which are known to elicit strong escape responses in mice (De Franceschi et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The distribution of values for escape response metrics overlapped considerably for naïve vs. implanted mice.
source: The distribution of values for the metrics tested (mean/max velocity and max acceleration) again overlapped considerably for naïve vs. implanted mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A few naive mice achieved max acceleration during escapes at values unobserved in implanted mice.
source: Although we observed no significant changes, a few naive mice achieved max acceleration during their escapes at values unobserved in implanted mice (Figure 3E, right).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Implanted mice remained active in an open arena and showed species-typical responses to threatening stimuli.
source: Taken together, these behavioral observations argue that although the presence of the AMIE may have idiosyncratically slowed mice slightly, they remained active in an open arena and showed species-typical responses to threatening stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data in Figure 3.

claim: The authors isolated ~60–100 units for each session in an experiment with the probe implanted in medial visual cortex, subiculum, and midbrain.
source: We isolated ~60–100 units for each session in this experiment (Figure 4D,E), during which the mouse moved freely around the arena and was exposed to looming stimuli.
evidence: This is a report of the number of units isolated, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The number of single units isolated ranged across mice and experiments from ~20 to 145.
source: The number of single units we were able to isolate ranged across mice and experiments from ~20 to 145, but these numbers were fairly consistent within each mouse across recording sessions (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a report of the range of units isolated, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The variability in number of isolated units is likely dependent on the probe used, recording noise, and brain region.
source: This variability is likely dependent on the probe that was used (Phase 3A Option four probes used in mouse #3 and #4 had 270 rather than 374 recordable channels; see Materials and methods and Jun et al., 2017), recording noise, and brain region.
evidence: This is an inference about the factors affecting unit yield.

claim: The absolute number of isolated units depends on the quality of the sorting and the experimenter's manual curation of Kilosort output.
source: The absolute number of isolated units depends on the quality of the sorting and the experimenter's manual curation of Kilosort output, which does present challenging edge cases and can be difficult to assess with drift in the experiment.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological factors affecting unit counts.

claim: The unit yields reported are less than has been previously reported with acute experiments in mice.
source: Overall, these numbers are less than has been previously reported with acute experiments in mice (Jun et al., 2017), possibly because of the chronic recording environment or inability to completely reduce noise.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work supported by citation.

claim: The longest the authors left a probe in was 41 days, without any noticeable decay in the signal.
source: The longest we left a probe in was 41 days, without any noticeable decay in the signal.
evidence: This is a report of the maximum duration tested.

claim: Waveforms were consistent in both shape and depth across recordings.
source: However, we did indeed observe waveforms that were consistent in both shape and depth across recordings, and it is entirely possible that these originate from the same neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Kilosort2 identified 77 well-isolated units for mouse #7, compared to 69 with Kilosort1 and manual post-Kilosort designations.
source: Indeed, for mouse #7, Kilosort2 identified 77 well-isolated units, compared to 69 with Kilosort1 and manual post-Kilosort designations in phy, confirming that our manual criteria were effective.
evidence: This is a comparison of sorting methods.

claim: The AMIE design enables researchers to implant a headbar to restrain the animal.
source: A major limitation of many chronic implant designs is that they do not enable researchers to also implant a headbar to restrain the animal.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the AMIE design.

claim: The ability to head-fix animals allows the experimenter to easily restrain the mouse during experiments.
source: The ability to head-fix animals critical for two reasons. First, it allows the experimenter to easily restrain the mouse during experiments, for example to attach/replace the headstage or fix twisting in the tether.
evidence: This is a practical advantage of the design.

claim: Head-fixing affords the opportunity to measure neural activity in response to traditional psychophysical stimuli after the freely moving recording.
source: Moreover, it affords the opportunity to measure neural activity in response to traditional psychophysical stimuli after the freely moving recording (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: After six days of recording freely moving behavior, the authors presented a battery of visual stimuli while the mouse was head-fixed.
source: For example, after six days of recording freely moving behavior, we presented a battery of visual stimuli while the mouse was head-fixed to determine whether cells were visually responsive (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 5.

claim: The authors were able to isolate 60 units in the restrained condition, just as in the freely moving condition.
source: We were able to isolate 60 units (63 with Kilosort2) in the restrained condition, just as in the freely moving condition (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a report of the number of units isolated, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells deep in the midbrain showed clear visual responses to drifting gratings during headfixed experiments.
source: Remarkably, during our headfixed experiments we found that even cells deep in the midbrain showed clear visual responses to drifting gratings (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The authors were able to record from a mouse for over 2 weeks, explant the probe, and re-implant for a second experiment.
source: We were able to record from a mouse for over 2 weeks, explant the probe, and re-implant for a second experiment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The re-implanted probe yielded 43.6 ± 17.8 neurons.
source: Still, the re-implanted probe yielded 43.6 ± 17.8 neurons which is ample for many studies, especially those conducted in labs for which Neuropixels probes are a scarce resource.
evidence: This is a report of the number of neurons isolated from the re-implanted probe.

claim: In another experiment, the authors were able to explant a probe from a mouse that did not recover from surgery and reimplant it in a second mouse.
source: In another experiment, were able to explant a probe from a mouse that did not recover from surgery and reimplant it in a second mouse (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of an experimental outcome shown in Table 1.

claim: One successful session of recording from a re-implanted probe yielded 145 units.
source: Although this second mouse ultimately also had complications resulting from a poorly positioned ground wire, one successful session of recording yielded 145 units (Figure 4C; Table 1).
evidence: This is a report of the number of units isolated, shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: There was a drop in the event rate in the re-implanted probe compared to the first implant.
source: There was a drop in the event rate and a small drop in the SNR in the re-implanted probe (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: There was a small drop in the SNR in the re-implanted probe compared to the first implant.
source: There was a drop in the event rate and a small drop in the SNR in the re-implanted probe (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: There was a significant drop in both event rate and SNR on the 12th day of recording in the first implant.
source: However, even with the first implant there was a significant drop in both event rate and SNR on the 12th day of recording, suggesting that this may not be due to the re-implantation itself.
evidence: This is an observation from the data that provides context for the re-implantation results.

claim: Applying silicone to the base of the shank to add extra support appears to be necessary for successful explant.
source: First, applying silicone to the base of the shank to add extra support appears to be necessary (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental outcomes.

claim: With silicone added to the base of the shank, 4/4 explant attempts were successful.
source: With silicone added to the base of the shank, 4/4 explant attempts were successful, whereas 1/6 explants were successful without the silicone (Table 1).
evidence: This is a report of the success rates shown in Table 1.

claim: Without silicone added to the base of the shank, 1/6 explants were successful.
source: With silicone added to the base of the shank, 4/4 explant attempts were successful, whereas 1/6 explants were successful without the silicone (Table 1).
evidence: This is a report of the success rates shown in Table 1.

claim: The authors only had success explanting Phase 3A Option three probes.
source: Third, we only had success with Phase 3A Option three probes, suggesting that it may be easier with these, possibly due to the fact that the recording shanks on these probes are longer (10 mm) than Option 1 (5 mm).
evidence: This is a report of the experimental outcomes.

claim: The shank of Phase 3B probes is 10 mm long.
source: Fortunately, the shank of Phase 3B probes (now on the market) is also 10 mm long.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the Phase 3B probes.

claim: The AMIE allows researchers to perform recordings in both restrained and unrestrained conditions.
source: Our device, the AMIE, and accompanying methods, allow researchers to perform recordings in both restrained and unrestrained conditions, and critically, to explant and reuse probes after experiments.
evidence: This is a summary of the capabilities demonstrated in the paper.

claim: The AMIE allows researchers to explant and reuse probes after experiments.
source: Our device, the AMIE, and accompanying methods, allow researchers to perform recordings in both restrained and unrestrained conditions, and critically, to explant and reuse probes after experiments.
evidence: This is a summary of the capabilities demonstrated in the paper.

claim: The AMIE has a slim enclosure for the probe as well as the headstage that mice can easily handle.
source: The AMIE has a slim enclosure for the probe as well as the headstage (Figures 1 and 2), that mice can easily handle (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the design and its validation shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The Neuropixels 3B (Neuropixels 1.0) version is the one currently commercially available.
source: It is worth noting that the Neuropixels design featured here is 3A, but the 3B (Neuropixels 1.0) version is the one currently commercially available.
evidence: This is factual information about the commercially available version.

claim: AMIE designs for both Neuropixels 3A and 3B probe generations are available in the resources for this paper.
source: AMIE designs for both probe generations are available in the resources for this paper (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the availability of resources.

claim: The AMIE design can be readily adapted to other types of silicon probes.
source: Our design can also be readily adapted to other types of silicon probes (e.g. Neuronexus).
evidence: This is a statement about the adaptability of the design.

claim: The current Neuropixels recording tether is not easily commutated due to heavy data demands.
source: Unlike other electrophysiology systems, the current Neuropixels recording tether is not easily commutated due to heavy data demands.
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the Neuropixels system.

claim: Recording from chronically-implanted rats in large arenas with Neuropixels has not been a problem despite the non-commutated tether.
source: While this has not been a problem for recording from chronically-implanted rats in large arenas (Jun et al., 2017), it can be challenging for recordings from mice in smaller arenas, requiring constant monitoring of the mouse's position and occasional intervention from the experimenter to untangle the cord.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work supported by citation.

claim: Recording from mice in smaller arenas with Neuropixels can be challenging, requiring constant monitoring and occasional intervention to untangle the cord.
source: While this has not been a problem for recording from chronically-implanted rats in large arenas (Jun et al., 2017), it can be challenging for recordings from mice in smaller arenas, requiring constant monitoring of the mouse's position and occasional intervention from the experimenter to untangle the cord.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experience.

claim: In the authors' experience, an hour-long session requires stopping once or twice to unplug the cord and untangle.
source: In our experience, this is manageable, requiring the experimenter to stop an hour-long session once or twice to unplug the cord and untangle.
evidence: This is a report of the authors' practical experience.

claim: The Neuropixels AMIE can be used to record in both restrained and unrestrained conditions, with similar yields in numbers of isolated units.
source: The Neuropixels AMIE can be used to record in both restrained and unrestrained conditions, with similar yields in numbers of isolated units (Figures 4 and 5), although a direct comparison of yields across publications is challenging due to potential differences in spike sorting criteria across labs.
evidence: This is a summary of the results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The ability to restrain the mouse for passive stimulation enables researchers to obtain additional information about their recordings.
source: The ability to restrain the mouse for passive stimulation enables researchers to obtain additional information about their recordings that may ultimately aid in uncovering the function of cells and brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the design.

claim: Male 3–4 month old C57/BL6 mice were used in the experiments.
source: We used male 3–4 month old C57/BL6 mice (Jackson Laboratories, 000664).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Male mice were used because they are typically larger and expected to better handle the weight of the implant.
source: Male mice were used because they are typically larger, and we expected that they would better handle the weight of the implant.
evidence: This is an explanation of the choice of experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were given medicated (carprofen) food cups 1–2 days prior to surgery.
source: Mice were given medicated (carprofen) food cups (MediGel CPF, Clear H20 74-05-5022) 1–2 days prior to surgery.
evidence: This is a description of the pre-surgical care.

claim: DiI signals could be found in the brain even 1 month after implantation.
source: We were able to find DiI signals in the brain even 1 month after implantation (we did not test later time points).
evidence: This is a report of the histological findings.
